source.title: KAP: Bridging the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption Gap in LLM Systems
source.summary: Modern LLM systems increasingly rely on knowledge-selection processes that produce high-value structured priors, such as ranked evidence, graph topology, multimodal alignment, and confidence signals. Yet LLM serving remains fundamentally oblivious to this rich structure: once such signals are serialized into a prompt, the backend observes only a flat token sequence, forcing dense and uniform consumption of the full key-value (KV) state during decoding. We term this architectural mismatch the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption (KSRC) gap: richer contexts enlarge the full-prompt KV footprint and decode-time memory traffic, increasing latency and degrading throughput even when reasoning depends on only a small fraction of the context. To bridge the gap, we propose Knowledge Access Planning (KAP), a paradigm-shifting execution abstraction that elevates structured knowledge priors from passive prompt-construction hints into first-class physical execution artifacts. KAP establishes a universal intermediate representation (IR)-the runtime access plan-which compiles structured knowledge signals to govern physical KV access without altering logical prompt semantics, model weights, or training procedures. Through this IR, KAP shifts LLM serving from token-aware context consumption to plan-driven, knowledge-aware runtime consumption. We instantiate KAP with GraphSpec, a compiler-executor realization connecting structured knowledge selection to an LLM serving backend. We derive a phase-boundary model for the positive-speedup regime of plan-guided execution. Across 4K-128K long-context QA workloads, GraphSpec maintains answer quality comparable to full-context decoding while decoupling physical KV consumption from prompt length, reducing proposal-time KV access to 5.5% of source KV state at 128K, and fundamentally shifting the scaling trajectory of long-context generation.

previous_facts.title: KAP: Bridging the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption Gap in LLM Systems
previous_facts.event_hint: KAP paradigm introduction: Knowledge Access Planning for LLM serving with GraphSpec implementation
previous_facts.problem: The Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption (KSRC) gap: LLM serving backends receive only serialized prompts, losing structured knowledge priors (ranked evidence, graph topology, multimodal alignment, confidence signals) from upstream selection processes. This forces uniform full-context KV consumption regardless of actual knowledge importance, increasing latency and degrading throughput as contexts lengthen.
previous_facts.mechanism: Knowledge Access Planning (KAP) elevates structured knowledge priors to first-class execution artifacts through a universal intermediate representation (runtime access plan). The IR encodes selected knowledge units, runtime object mappings, logical positions, access policy, and verification policy. Instantiated as GraphSpec with Graph-RAG frontend and VLLM backend, using compiler-executor architecture to translate structured priors into KV access plans without altering model weights, training, or logical prompt semantics.

evidence.claim: GraphSpec reduces proposal-time KV access to 5.5% of source KV state at 128K context length while maintaining answer quality comparable to full-context decoding
evidence.condition: 128K-token long-context QA workload, proposal-time KV access metric

evidence.claim: GraphSpec achieves 1.19x decode-throughput speedup at 128K context length versus full-context decoding
KAP decouples physical KV consumption from prompt length, fundamentally shifting long-context generation scaling trajectory
evidence.baseline: linear physical cost growth with context length

evidence.claim: GraphSpec instantiation connects Graph-RAG knowledge-selection frontend to VLLM LLM serving backend

previous_facts.evaluation_context: Long-context QA workloads spanning 4K to 128K token contexts. Knowledge-selection frontend uses Graph-RAG to produce structured priors (graph topology, ranked evidence). LLM serving backend uses VLLM. Evaluation metrics include proposal-time KV access percentage, decode throughput speedup, and answer quality comparison to full-context decoding baseline. No hardware platform, latency absolute values, or deployment scale visible in evidence pack.
previous_facts.limitations: Evaluation limited to long-context QA workloads; generalization to other task types (code generation, multi-turn dialogue, agentic workflows) not addressed in visible evidence. Verification/fallback overhead not quantified. Phase-boundary model presented but positive-speedup regime conditions not fully specified in abstract/introduction. GraphSpec is one concrete instantiation; KAP paradigm generality claimed but only Graph-RAG+VLLM combination demonstrated.
previous_facts.project_relevance: Directly addresses AI infra horizontal dynamics question: which systems/hardware changes affect end-to-end efficiency. KAP introduces execution-time planning layer between knowledge selection and LLM serving, potentially reducing GPU memory bandwidth pressure and improving throughput for RAG systems. Relevant to serving-runtime optimization direction. However, missing production deployment data and hardware-specific benchmarking limit immediate actionability. Should be tracked as infra-level optimization paradigm; may warrant dedicated topic if adoption emerges in production serving stacks.
